chapter_theme: A single song at Keeranur (கீரனூர்): the courtesans' arts of luring and pricing, and the churning of the milk sea in praise of Vishnu as Murugan's uncle.

952.reading: The poet lists what courtesans do: laugh with charm, melt men with song and dance, call anyone at all, wound with Kama's eyes, stand at the doorway in the street, name a price, sway their breasts, loosen and tie their hair, let their garments slip, speak desire, fall on a man and leave him in great sorrow; he asks whether kinship with women who learn these arts of deceit is fit for him. The praise tells the churning of the milk sea, Meru as the churning stick and the serpent as rope, Vali holding half and the gods the other half, until Lakshmi, the Parijata and many powers rose, and names Murugan nephew of the green Achyuta who gave out the nectar, the bearer of the vel at Keeranur, a town of mansions and groves like Kubera's Alaka.
952.nuance: விலைகூறி: naming a price is the plainest courtesan charge, and தோதக வித்தைகள், arts of deceit, are something learned. In the churning, பாதி வாலி பிடித்திட gives Vali the place usually held by the demons.

links.note: Both describe the courtesan's charm as calculated: the Kural's women weigh the profit before speaking of their virtue, and in 952 they name the price and learn their arts of deceit.
